verdicts.issue: Source: 'As the whole dark earth bows before some tempest ... even such was the stress and strain of the Trojan horses'. AFTER states the storm as a plain fact ('The whole dark earth bows before a tempest...') and then 'Such was the stress...', so the 'as when... so...' simile frame is lost.
verdicts.fix: Patroclus kept steering his horses toward wherever he saw the most men fleeing in confusion, cheering on his men as he went. Chariots were being smashed in all directions, and many a man tumbled from his own car and fell beneath the wheels of Patroclus’s chariot. Its immortal horses, which the gods had given to Peleus, sprang over the trench in a single bound as they raced on. Patroclus was set on getting near Hector, for he had his heart fixed on spearing him, but Hector’s horses were now hurrying him away. As the whole dark earth bows before a tempest on an autumn day, when Zeus rains his hardest to punish men who give crooked judgments in their courts, drive justice out of them and ignore the decrees of heaven, and all the rivers run full, and the torrents tear many a new channel as they roar headlong from the mountains to the dark sea, and it goes badly for the works of men, so great was the stress and strain of the Trojan horses in their flight.

verdicts.issue: Source: 'Let be, my friends' (leave me alone, let me go). AFTER 'Let it be, my friends' reads as 'drop it / accept it' and changes the sense of Priam's plea.
verdicts.fix: So the head of Hector was dishonored in the dust. His mother tore her hair and flung her veil away with a loud cry when she saw her son. His father groaned piteously, and all through the city the people began to weep and wail. It was as if the whole of frowning Ilium were smoldering in fire. The people could hardly hold Priam back, so hot was his haste to rush out of the city gates. He groveled in the mire and begged them, calling each one by name. “Let me be, my friends,” he cried, “and for all your sorrow, allow me to go alone to the ships of the Achaeans. Let me plead with this cruel and terrible man. Perhaps he will respect the feelings of his fellow men and have pity on my old age. His own father is just such another as I am—Peleus, who bred him and raised him to be the bane of us Trojans, and of me more than of all others. He has killed many a son of mine in the flower of his youth. Yet however I grieve for those, I grieve for one—Hector—more than for them all, and the bitterness of my sorrow will bring me down to the house of Hades. I wish he had died in my arms. Then both his ill-starred mother who bore him and I would have had the comfort of weeping and mourning over him.”
